resources.string: This application was created to demonstrate the methods of detecting VPN and Proxy according to the officially approved methodology. The tool is designed to show that to hide the fact of circumvention, a comprehensive approach is required, bypassing a set of independent checks.
Server-side analysis. Comparison of IP with reputation databases.
Comparison of IPv4 and IPv6 geolocations to detect bypass traffic.
Querying the Android billing API for TRANSPORT_VPN and VpnTransportInfo.
Detecting proxy settings based on System.getProperty system properties.
Search for installed known VPN/Proxy clients and bypass tools.
Checking for the NET_CAPABILITY_NOT_VPN flag in active network connections.
Search for virtual tunneling adapters (tun, tap, wg, ppp).
Analysis of frame size (MTU) for traces of VPN header encapsulation.
Checking standard ports (Socks5/HTTP) opened by client proxies.
Checking if fake local IP addresses are returned to domains (Fake-IP tunneling).
Comparison of ping to local and remote nodes.
Analyzing if IP belongs to a hosting service/datacenter (IP Type verification).
The method determines the IP region on the server side (GeoIP).

Configure Split Tunneling in your VPN client settings (such as Amnezia VPN, v2rayNG, OpenVPN, WireGuard) and add this application to the exclusion list (Bypass/Excluded Apps). This routes the application\'s traffic directly through the physical WAN interface, bypassing the virtual VPN connection and returning the correct local IP.
Circumvention is reliably hidden at the GeoIP level.
Could not retrieve server response with GeoIP.
The system directly reports an active VPN tunnel.

Use user-space tunneling (User-space SOCKS5/HTTP Proxy, e.g., in-app Proxy Client mode in Daedalus/SagerNet), or leverage transparent proxying via iptables/nftables on a rooted device to bypass the VpnService API entirely.
Detection of system proxy usage based on System.getProperty system properties.

Reset global JVM proxy and APN proxy in system settings of your Access Point Name (APN), or clear system properties http.proxyHost and socksProxyHost via ADB/root command \'settings delete global http_proxy\'.
Indirect evidence. This flag is present in physical network connections and missing when VPN is active.

Switch the proxy client to pure TCP/UDP socket mode (e.g., SOCKS5 via shared socket libraries bypassing the OS) or apply traffic obfuscation (ByeDPI/TPWS) that acts on application sockets without overriding system Capabilities.
Indirect evidence. Presence of virtual interfaces (tun/tap/wg) may indicate a tunnel.

Route traffic via SOCKS5/HTTP proxy with built-in translation (such as gost or tun2socks in proxy-server mode without creating a tun interface), or rename the virtual interface in the kernel (via \'ip link set dev tun0 name eth1\') on a rooted device.
Indirect check of virtual tunnel adapters.
Direct evidence. Popular installed VPN clients detected.

Use custom-built VPN clients with modified package_name identifiers, place applications in a secure partition (Samsung Knox, Private Space in Android 15), or utilize Magisk/KernelSU with Shamiko / Hide My Applist to hide packages from PackageManager.
Check for popular installed VPN clients.
Indirect evidence. Lowered MTU is typical for tunneled traffic due to header encapsulation.

Set standard MTU (1500 for Wi-Fi/Ethernet, or 1410-1430 for mobile networks) in the tunnel configuration file (e.g., \'MTU = 1500\' in WireGuard profile) or configure backend-side MSS clamping to hide encapsulation overhead.
Analysis of frame size (MTU) for indirect traces of VPN encapsulation.
Indirect evidence. Open ports can indicate a local Proxy/Xray/Socks5 server is running.

Change the default incoming ports (1080, 10808, 9050) in your in-app proxy client JSON config (Xray/SagerNet/v2ray) to random high ports in the Ephemeral range (49152–65535) and bind to loopback (127.0.0.1) only.
Analysis of open local ports typical for proxy clients.
Indirect evidence. The VPN core (e.g. Xray/sing-box) spoofs IPs to intercept traffic.
Disable the Fake-IP mechanism in your client profile (e.g., in Clash/sing-box) and switch to Real-IP mode, configuring Direct-DNS routing or forwarding queries to a local recursive DNS resolver.
Checking for fake internal IP addresses mapping to popular servers (Fake-IP tunneling).
Indirect evidence. Usage of public/custom DNS servers (like Google, Cloudflare, etc.) or VPN DNS ranges suggests DNS routing detour.
Checking for custom, public (Google, Cloudflare, Quad9, etc.) or VPN-assigned DNS servers.

Turn off custom DNS/Private DNS in Android system settings, revert to automatic DNS from the ISP via DHCP/SLAAC, and instead use encrypted DNS tunnels (DoH/DoT) inside your VPN tunnel configuration without modifying global system resolvers.
Analysis of RTT to control landmarks.
Too low ping (<= 2ms) is impossible in real networks and indicates TCP intercept by a local proxy.
Add check hosts (google.com, cloudflare.com) to your routing exclusions (bypass-rules) in the proxy client, so that packet roundtrips bypass the local interception sockets and travel natively.
Abnormally high latency to local node compared to remote node indicates VPN usage.

Connect to ultra-low latency entry nodes closest to your physical location, use lightweight protocols (WireGuard/AmneziaWG instead of OpenVPN TCP), or configure direct routing exemptions for latency-measured host addresses.
Comparing ping (TCP RTT) for local and remote nodes.
LEAK! IPv4 is encrypted (%1$s), but IPv6 goes directly (%2$s, Country: %3$s)
CLEAN (IPv6: %1$s, but country not defined - leak unlikely)
CLEAN (IPv6 connection did not return address)
CLEAN (IPv6 is not supported or blocked by tunnel)
Determining real IPv6 address leak. Common VPN vulnerability where IPv6 traffic goes around the tunnel.
Analysis of real IPv6 address leak via unprotected routes.

Enable the \'Block Non-VPN Traffic\' or \'::/0 forced redirect\' option inside your VPN client settings, disable IPv6 entirely in the mobile APN profile on your Android device, or turn off IPv6 on your home router (SLAAC/DHCPv6).
Checking if your IP address is a known cloud hosting, secondary VPN provider exit, SOCKS proxy egress node or Tor node.
Checking if the client IP belongs to a cloud datacenter or hosting network node.

Use a residential proxy egress server (Residential IP Proxy / ISP proxy) or residential VPN tunnel that routes traffic through home consumer ISPs (such as Comcast, ISP, Telecom) rather than cloud servers (like DigitalOcean, AWS, Hetzner, OVH).
Methodology of detecting signs of bypass tools usage on client devices. Recognized text in Markdown format.
Please select your preferred app language and target GeoIP region to start. The target region is the country you expect to be geolocated in when no VPN is active.
Country code must be exactly 2 letters (e.g. US)

Configure which tests run during scanning (for experienced users).
Using independent GeoIP providers. Additional requests are sent to external latency nodes (SNITCH) to measure network delays. See details in the Info tab.

To perform scanning and analyze connection quality, independent public services are used:

• sypexgeo.net, ipify.org, ipapi.is, ipapi.co, ipwho.is, freeipapi.com — external GeoIP API providers to determine your current IP and check for route leaks.

• google.com — latency testing endpoint for measuring round-trip time (RTT/SNITCH).

• ya.ru (Yandex) — additional latency endpoint used specifically when target region is set to Russia (RU) to detect traffic routing anomalies indicating the presence of a bypass tool.
